text:
When I arrived at the station, the last bus had already left. I had planned to visit my aunt, who lived in a village outside the town. She had invited me to stay for the weekend because she needed help in her garden. I tried to call her, but my phone had no power left.

At first I thought about walking. The village was only six kilometres away, and I knew the road well. However, it was getting dark, and heavy clouds were moving towards the town. I decided to ask for help at the small shop beside the station.

The woman behind the counter let me use her phone. My aunt was worried because she had expected me an hour earlier. I explained what had happened and said I was safe. She could not collect me herself because her car was being repaired. Her neighbour offered to drive instead.

While I waited, I bought a sandwich and talked to the woman in the shop. She told me that the bus times had changed the week before. The old timetable was still on the station wall. I had checked that timetable rather than the new one online.

My aunt's neighbour arrived just as the rain began. I thanked the woman for her help and ran to his car. During the journey, we agreed that someone should replace the old timetable. Otherwise, other visitors might make the same mistake. By the time we reached the village, my aunt had made tea. I was late, but I was pleased that I had asked for help instead of walking in the storm.

text:
For a long time, I believed that a good friend should always tell the truth. Then my brother asked me what I thought of the picture he had painted. He had worked on it for weeks and was clearly proud of it. I did not like the colours, but I could see how much effort he had made.

I could have said that the picture was wonderful. That would have made him happy for a moment. Yet he had asked for my opinion, and a false answer would not help him improve. I could also have said that I did not like it at all. That answer would have been honest, but it would have hidden the things he had done well.

In the end, I told him that I liked the trees and the shape of the house. I also said that the sky looked too dark to me. He was quiet for a while. Then he explained that he wanted the scene to feel sad. I had thought he was trying to show a cheerful summer day. Once I understood his aim, I looked at the picture differently.

This did not make every colour right in my eyes. We still disagreed about some parts. But it reminded me that honesty is more than saying the first thing that comes into your head. You also need to listen. If you do not understand what another person is trying to do, your advice may be less useful than you think.

I still believe that friends should tell each other the truth. I no longer think that a quick answer is always the most honest one. Sometimes a question is a better place to begin.
